opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the lottery ticket framing gives a really intuitive way to think about it. If you take the view that what training is partly doing is finding a good subnetwork, some sparse configuration of weights that's already well-positioned at initialization, then overparameterization is essentially buying you more lottery tickets. The bigger the network, the more possible subnetworks are embedded inside it, and the higher the chance that at least one of them starts out in a good spot relative to the task.

That was one of the things that surprised us in the supermask work. We found that you could take a randomly initialized network, never train the weights at all, and just learn a mask over them, and still get performance well above chance. Sometimes surprisingly well. That suggests a large random network already contains a lot of useful functions, and the job of optimization is as much about selecting as about building.

So from that perspective, overparameterization isn't wasted capacity. It makes the search easier. With a small network you have to get lucky with your initialization, or the optimizer has to do a lot of work moving weights into the right configuration. With a large network the landscape is richer, there are many more paths to a good solution, and gradient descent can sort of latch onto the ones that are already promising.

I'd add a caveat, though. I don't think "training is just finding a subnetwork" is the full story. Weights do move during training, and that movement matters, especially for reaching the best performance. Pruning experiments also show that the winning subnetworks often depend on some early training, not purely on initialization. So I'd see it as a useful lens rather than a complete theory. But it explains a lot about why bigger models can be easier to train, even when they have far more parameters than they strictly need.

r001.rationale: The response suggests useful subnetworks may exist at initialization, but does not state that theoretical work establishes their existence in sufficiently overparameterized models.

r002.rationale: It says a bigger network contains more possible subnetworks and raises the chance that at least one is well positioned for the task.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it comes a lot from the lottery ticket work. The lottery ticket hypothesis says that inside a big randomly initialized network, there exist these sparse subnetworks that, if you train them in isolation from their original initialization, reach roughly the same accuracy as the full network. And once you take that seriously, you can reframe what training is doing. Rather than thinking of gradient descent as sculpting one big function, you can think of it as implicitly searching over a huge space of candidate subnetworks and amplifying the ones that happen to be useful.

Under that view, overparameterization is essentially about having more lottery tickets. If your network is tiny, you have very few subnetworks, and the chance that any of them starts out in a good basin, with a good combination of weights and signs, is low. If your network is huge, you have combinatorially many subnetworks, so it becomes very likely that some of them are already pretty good at initialization, and optimization just needs to find and strengthen them while suppressing the rest. So the benefit is really a benefit in the search space, not in the final model you need. The final model can be small. It's the search that needs the width.

Something that pushed me toward this framing was the follow-up work I did on what actually matters in a winning ticket. We found that you don't need the exact initialization values to retrain a ticket successfully. What matters is largely the signs of the weights. If you keep the mask and keep the signs, you can reinitialize the magnitudes and it still works. That told me that what the big network is giving you is a sort of combinatorial coverage over sign patterns and connectivity patterns, and the winning ticket is one configuration out of that space that's already aligned with the task.

And then the supermask results take this even further. You can find masks over a random, untrained network that, with no weight training at all, get meaningfully above chance accuracy on something like MNIST. That's search in its purest form. You're not changing the weights, you're just selecting which ones to keep. So the fact that that works at all is pretty strong evidence that a lot of the "learning" we attribute to gradient descent is really selection among things that were already present, and overparameterization is what makes that selection possible.

I'd caveat that it's a lens, not a complete theory. Gradient descent obviously does change weights, and the dynamics matter. But I find it a useful way to think about why bigger helps even when the thing you end up with could have been expressed with far fewer parameters.

r001.rationale: The response says the lottery ticket hypothesis claims that useful subnetworks exist in large networks, but it does not state that theoretical work establishes this.

r002.rationale: It explains that larger networks provide combinatorially more subnetworks, making it more likely that some are good at initialization.

astra-6.text:
One way to think about it is that a larger network gives you more possible subnetworks to search over. So the benefit of overparameterization isn’t necessarily that you need all of those parameters to represent a good solution. It may be that having those extra parameters makes a good solution easier to find through training.

That’s the intuition behind the lottery ticket perspective: a large, randomly initialized network contains smaller subnetworks that, with the right initialization, can train well on their own. Making the network larger gives you more opportunities to contain one of those successful subnetworks.

The caveat is that gradient descent isn’t explicitly enumerating subnetworks. The parameters interact during training, so this is a useful perspective on why additional capacity can help optimization, rather than a complete explanation of what training is doing.

r001.rationale: The response says a large randomly initialized network can contain subnetworks that train well, but does not state that theoretical work establishes this in a sufficiently overparameterized model.

r002.rationale: It explains that making the network larger creates more opportunities to contain a successful subnetwork, conveying that more available combinations increase the chance of finding one.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to think about it is that, when we train a large network, we’re also searching for a subnetwork that can solve the task. Overparameterization gives us a much larger collection of possible subnetworks to search over. So the benefit isn’t necessarily that the final solution needs all those parameters; it’s that having more parameters makes a good solution easier to find.

That changes how you interpret pruning, for example. If you can remove most of the weights after training and retain performance, that doesn’t mean those extra weights were unnecessary during training. They may have provided the flexibility that allowed optimization to discover that particular solution. Finding a small network inside a large one can be much easier than training a small network directly.

r001.rationale: The response describes searching a large network for a good subnetwork, but does not state that theoretical work establishes such a subnetwork exists in a sufficiently overparameterized model.

r002.rationale: It says overparameterization creates a much larger collection of possible subnetworks, making a good solution easier to find.
